Q: Table-based testing A:

I would treat this as an indexing problem rather than a prompt problem.

For table-heavy HR documents, don’t chunk tables the same way as prose. Extract each table separately and keep row-level records with metadata such as document id, page, section heading, table caption, row index, and column names.

Then index at two levels:

- table level: caption, surrounding section text, and a short table summary

- row level: a readable serialization of each row, while preserving the original structured fields

For queries asking for a list or comparison, retrieve candidate tables first, then fetch the relevant rows from those tables. Hybrid search is useful here because many HR questions contain exact terms like role names, regions, policy names, or benefit types. Pure vector search can miss those.

The LLM should only synthesize from the retrieved structured rows and citations. If retrieval cannot identify a complete table or row set, it is better to return insufficient evidence than to let the model infer missing rows.

Q: EC2 error: cannot create temp file for here-document: Read-only file system A:

Maybe you don't have write permission to the /tmp/ directory.

Check permission and it should be look like 

ls -ld /tmp  
drwxrwxrwt 10 root root 4096 Jun  5 11:32 /tmp

You can fix the permissions followed by 

chmod a+rwxt /tmp

Q: Create a friend request system A:

I was totally wrong, you don't need to create any extra flag, just store the user_id -which you retrieve from the database when the user logs in - store it in the session then when he/she clicks on the add friend button check the $_SESSION['user_id'] with the id of the other user before completing the friendship function, if they're both the same, means it's the same person, otherwise add friends.

Q: Swap out a low-level dependency A:

Swapping dependencies based on a grand parent is typically a hard problem for DI Containers.

DI Containers like Simple Injector and Ninject have explicit support for conditionally or context-based registering dependencies based on the consuming type. Ninject contains a .WhenInjectedInto method for this, where Simple Injector provides a RegisterConditional method. However, where Ninject allows you to look up the parent hierarchy and base the dependency on the grand parent (your use case), the Simple Injector designers (which includes me) decided not to allow allow registrations to look further up than their direct parent, because "making a decision based on the parent’s parent can lead to all sorts of complications and subtle bugs." This especially happens when the intermediate dependency (AddressFormatter in your case) gets a lifestyle other than Transient as it could lead to Torn and Ambiguous Lifestyles.

Although this explanation doesn't solve your issue, it hopefully gives some background information on what issues can arise from grand-parent based conditional registration.

For MS.DI, the built-in DI Container, however, things get worse, because there is not even support for doing context-based injection through its API.

To solve this, there are multiple workarounds.

Workaround 1: Register the graph completely by hand

services.AddTransient<CustomerFileController>(sp =>
    new CustomerFileController(
        formatter: new AddressFormatter(
            dataWriter: new FileDataWriter())));

services.AddTransient<CustomerDatabaseController>(sp =>
    new CustomerDatabaseController(
        formatter: new AddressFormatter(
            dataWriter: new DatabaseDataWriter())));

This method, however, gets pretty tedious and maintenance heavy, because as the object graph changes, so does this registration. Further more, when dependencies need different lifestyles, it becomes even harder.

A better workaround would, therefore, be a mix between manual registration and auto-wiring.

Workaround 2: Mix auto-wiring with hand-wiring the object graph

container.AddSingleton<FileDataWriter>();
container.AddSingleton<DatabaseDataWriter>();

services.AddTransient<CustomerFileController>(() =>
    ActivatorUtilitie.CreateInstance<CustomerFileController>(sp,
        ActivatorUtilitie.CreateInstance<AddressFormatter>(sp,
            sp.GetRequiredService<FileDataWriter>())));

services.AddTransient<CustomerDatabaseController>(() =>
    ActivatorUtilitie.CreateInstance<CustomerFileController>(sp,
        ActivatorUtilitie.CreateInstance<AddressFormatter>(sp,
            sp.GetRequiredService<DatabaseDataWriter>())));

This code uses ActivatorUtilitie, which is part of the MS.DI library. The CreateInstance allows creating, in this case, new AddressFormatter, CustomerFileController, and CustomerFileController instances, where all their dependencies are resolved from the supplied service provider (sp), where any supplied dependency is preferred over any dependency from the service provider.

From maintainability, this is much better, even though changes to AddressFormatter's constructor and those to the controllers' constructors are made, this code keeps working without having to make changes.

Still, there are some caveats here, as CreateInstance will always create a new instance, effectively making the class transient.

Another issue with ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance is that it circumvents the containers cyclic dependency detection. Where MS.DI will (typically) warn you when you registered a cyclic dependency graph, this detection easily goes out the way whenever you start using ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance in the registration process, which will result in stack-overflow exceptions instead. I learned this the hard way and this has costed me many hours already.

There are many other workarounds, such as making use of keyed registration i.c.w. attributes and also sub typing. But I consider those less practical for your particular case.
